Alternatively, if for some reason it's not possible or not desirable to put all initialization in the constructor, I would recommend we make the constructors protected/private and use something like a factory pattern to produce them. The user/developer would not be able to construct a sensor in an uninitialized state, and the factory would be responsible for ensuring that it is fully initialized before being provided to a user/developer.

I try to explain what I think it's happening here:

 - `ign-gazebo` is linking against camera from `ign-sensor` in the Sensor.cc. This is the [CMakeLists.txt](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-gazebo/blob/master/src/systems/sensors/CMakeLists.txt#L7). When the program starts then the symbols from `libignition-gazebo4-sensors-system.so` are loaded which also includes `libignition-sensors4-camera.so` because as I explained before the CMake is linking with the sensor library.

 - This same file (Sensor.cc) is loading the camera plugin (`libignition-sensors4-camera.so`) using dlsym, In this [line of code](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-gazebo/blob/master/src/systems/sensors/Sensors.cc#L476) if there is a `<sensor name="camera" type="camera">` in the sdf file. **Here is where the problem arises**

The Macro `IGN_SENSORS_REGISTER_SENSOR(CameraSensor)` is creating a [struct in an anonymous namespace](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-plugin/blob/master/register/include/ignition/plugin/detail/Register.hh#L445-L463). Inside this namespace a static variable is created which is in charge of loading the symbols. The first time that this struct is generated is when the class is called (linked by the CMake) but the second time that we need to read the symbols (in the "createSensor" method) then this static variable is no being initialized again. 

I have create a simple demo to reproduce this [here](https://github.com/ahcorde/mini_test).

The right example to hace a look is ` ./main_dl_link_cmake`. This is doing exactely the same thing. 

The `hello` library contains a struct and a static variable inside an anonymous namespace. In the main this library is linked with cmake and then is being loaded using `dlsym()`. The text is only printed once and it should be printed twice

I think I found a solution. If the symbols are already loaded, why we need to reload it again? There is no need to do it.

I spoke with @nkoenig about how we want to go about implementing this. I'm trying to start with something trivial like the [LogicalCameraSensor](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-sensors/blob/master/include/ignition/sensors/LogicalCameraSensor.hh). I looked at OpenAL, and although it could be used to produce actual audio to something like computer speakers or headphones, there doesn't seem to be a way to programmatically determine whether or not a listener/microphone can hear sound emitted from a particular source or not (if a sound device can hear the audio, OpenAL will output sound, but if not, then you just won't hear anything emitting from your sound device).

So, in order to programmatically determine whether a microphone can actually hear an audio source at a certain location or not, I'm thinking I could go down the following route:
* Define a graph of audio objects, with an audio object being either a "microphone" or "source"
* In this graph, microphones can be connected to multiple sources, and sources can be connected to multiple microphones, but microphones cannot not be connected to other microphones, and sources cannot be connected to other sources
    - The cost of an edge between a source and microphone could be the euclidean distance of a straight line between the two objects (this wouldn't account for things like obstacles in the world, but we can find ways to create a better edge cost later)
    - If we wanted to connect microphones to other microphones or sources to other sources, then the edge costs of these connections can be infinity
* A microphone considers sound emitted from a source as "detected" if the sound pressure at the microphone is above a certain threshold
    - If we know the sound pressure emitted from the source (`p_1`) at a specific distance (`r_1`), then we can calculate the sound pressure (`p_2`) at the microphone's distance from the source (`r_2`) using `p_2 = ((r_1 / r_2) * p_1)` (this equation was pulled from [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_pressure#Inverse-proportional_law))

Through some debugging, I noticed that when building `ignition-rendering` with `brew`, the `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` environment variable includes `/usr/local`, which causes the `/usr/local/lib/libOgreOverlay.dylib` symbolic link to the ogre1.9 library to be preferred (since `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` is evaluated before `HINTS` in the `find_library` call used in `FindIgnOGRE2`). about the idea of parallelizng camera rendering, I'm not sure if OGRE supports this since there are orders of operations that must be done in sequence in OGRE to prepare the scene for rendering. If we try to make concurrent rendering calls, we usually run into problems locking hardware buffers and OGRE would crash. One workaround would be to distribute to multiple OGRE instances, each with their own GL context. But then there would be the tradeoff of sync'ing data between processes.

But before diving into this, I think it would help to profile (e.g. using [ign profiler](https://ignitionrobotics.org/api/common/3.6/profiler.html)) and see where the bottlenecks are. On the other hand, I've noticed things like if the VRAM is full, the RTF drops to half. We also found issues with lights (with large range) causing performance hit. So there are also a few other places for performance improvement.

Generally, there are 3 time-consuming parts:

1. RenderingSensor::Render (this could in theory be parallelized)
2. PostUpdate in simulator
3. Sensors::PostUpdate

I guess 2 and 3 can very well be just waiting until the render thread notifies it has finished. The rendering operation itself is actually allowed to run in parallel to the simulation continuing.  The only requirement is that the rendering must be complete before the next rendering call can start.

The first iteration in ign-gazebo had rendering sensors blocking all simulation, which was introducing a huge amount of latency.  This is in contrast to gazebo9/10/11, which allowed sensors to run freely in parallel with the simulation, at a potential simulation accuracy hit.

In cases where all of the cameras are at the same frame rate and syncronized, this provides some speedup by allowing the rendering to happen in parallel at the cost of a small bit of sensor latency.  If all the rendering sensors are at different rates and starting times, the benefit is lost.

All that being said, rendering should be profilable, if built with the flag enabled.  It may not have as many profile points, though.

And for clarity, "in parallel" here means the rendering thread works in parallel with the simulation thread.  Each rendering sensor that needs a frame generated will run in series in the rendering thread.

Some of the time in post-update may be read back from the GPU and serialization for ign-transport as well.

a little late but this sums it up:

>  My understanding is that there is a difference between what the camera can detect and the data that is produced.

* output range = [0, 255*3] K: this the range of possible values that can be generated by an 8 bit camera with a resolution of 3.
* [-inf, inf]: are the user specified `min` and `max` temperature values. 

e.g. user can limit the max temp produced by the camera by specifying something like [0, 200]. If the user specifies something like [0, 800], the max reading will be the min(800, 255*3), which is 765.

Additional features for sonars --

I debated whether to put this in the RaySensor close-the-gap ticket (https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-sensors/issues/26) or this one. I decided this one, because this ticket is for a sensor called sonar, while the RaySensor could be used for other things, even though users actually adapt the RaySensor to model sonars.

It has been raised that the ray / sonar sensors in Gazebo only return distances, while real sonar data depend on many other properties. To improve the sensor in Ignition, it would be great to support custom properties such as
- roughness
- material (not as in visual texture, but as in metal vs not metal, etc.)
- physical light scattering

and other things someone who actually uses sonars would be much more well-versed in than me.

We don't necessarily have to implement all of those (though that would be the ideal), but the idea is to have some kind of built-in support to make specifying a few properties easier (e.g. through plugin parameters, per-object custom SDF tags, etc.), without users having to each write their own plugins before having a simulated sensor that meets common expectations.

It would be interesting to add some more context about the use case for the sensor and what kind of data it should produce. I think it's especially important to define these clearly because this sensor wouldn't be replicating any real physical sensors. In the real world, this kind of data is obtained by operating on data provided by other sensors, like cameras.

> It would be interesting to add some more context about the use case for the sensor and what kind of data it should produce.

The original thought was to use this sensor to provide users with datasets that could be used for training machine learning models. Manually generating bounding boxes for images can be difficult and/or take a while, so the hope is that the process of data collection can be made easier by using this sensor with various scenes that are created in simulation.

Regarding what data it should produce: the thought is to provide users with an image and a corresponding bounding box message which provides the bounding box information for all of the requested objects in a scene (a new bounding box message type needs to be created in `ign-msgs`). The bounding box message can look similar to the [bounding box message type used in `darknet_ros`](https://github.com/leggedrobotics/darknet_ros/tree/master/darknet_ros_msgs/msg). So, once a user creates a simulation world and attaches labels to objects that the user wants bounding boxes for (see https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-gazebo/pull/853), an image would be captured of the scene and bounding box data would be specified for the objects in the scene requested by the user (assuming that the objects are visible, of course). To take this a step further, the scene could be altered (changing the camera position, object positions, lighting, etc.) to generate another image with bounding box data. If we add a way to programmatically alter the scene, this would allow users to quickly generate hundreds of various scenes with corresponding bounding box data.

> this sensor wouldn't be replicating any real physical sensors. In the real world, this kind of data is obtained by operating on data provided by other sensors, like cameras.

Yep :+1: this sensor is meant to provide a way for automatic bounding box generation so that users don't need to operate on data from things like cameras. As mentioned earlier in my comment, the main use case for this would probably be dataset generation for ML models, but perhaps users will find this useful for other use cases as well.

I'm not sure, but [bounding box messages in ROS](https://github.com/ros-perception/vision_msgs/blob/noetic-devel/msg/BoundingBox2D.msg) are oriented, so I think it's worth documenting the rationale for orienting it or not. As a reference, [here's some discussion](https://discourse.ros.org/t/proposal-new-computer-vision-message-standards/1819/) on the vision message standards for ROS that could be useful. The [vision_msgs README](https://github.com/ros-perception/vision_msgs) also has useful information.

> perhaps we can add in 3D functionality once the 2D implementation has been completed

My only concern is not to have to go back and change messages and APIs if we decide to support 3D later. If we want to leave the way open for it, we may want to use 3D types on the APIs for future-proofing.

I think that the first idea (GUI system) is fine. When you say `The GUI system will be using the rendering APIs`, does that include doing things like like changing the position of the objects in the scene? Because for doing things like changing an entity's position, that can actually be done in `ign-gazebo` with the `EntityComponentManager` (for the example of changing an entity's position, you'd need to modify the entity's pose component). So, can you provide a specific list of ideas that you have for `The GUI system will be using the rendering APIs`? If any of the tasks you have in mind can be done through `ign-gazebo` instead of `ign-rendering`, then it would probably be better to use the `ign-gazebo` APIs.

For the second idea (auto-generated datasets that use randomness and/or without much user control), I have a few comments:

> These randomness could be controlled by the user, for example by specifying a center and radius, and the tool will put the sensors in positions in the circle that is defined by that center and radius (I don't have much ideas about how to control that randomness)

Creating different camera positions/angles is one option. Here are a few other options:
1. Add/remove other objects in the scene. This would help reduce bias in the datasets, and discourage false positives from models that are trained on this data. For objects that may be worth adding/removing in scenes used for generating datasets, I'd recommend looking at the [Google Research fuel models](https://app.ignitionrobotics.org/GoogleResearch). There are a lot of photo-realistic models to choose from here.
2. Modify lighting and/or textures. This would allow for greater diversity in datasets without having to modify camera and/or object positions. You may want to look at the [light spawning gazebo plugin](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-gazebo/pull/587), which was added in Edifice and is also in Fortress (this light spawning plugin could also be used for the GUI system suggestion, along with adding GUI options for adding/modifying textures).

> I think that this approach may provide bad samples data, because it will show useless samples in some cases, and may collect the samples from a wrong view

I would actually argue that this approach of "randomness" could produce better datasets than human-generated datasets. When it comes to generating ML datasets, we want to remove as much bias from the data as possible. By viewing objects from various angles and having different objects in various images (based on what is visible and what is not), we are generating data that is more generalizable than data that only views objects under a pre-defined set of conditions. Another valuable aspect of the "randomness" approach is that a lot of data is generated quickly, compared to manual dataset generation, which usually takes a while.

Yes, I do agree with you that some samples in the generated data may be useless, and some human "data cleaning" may be needed once datasets are generated, but data cleaning is a normal part of the ML dataset collection process. In order to minimize the chance of generating useless data, we should implement some base-case checking on the backend for the auto-generation dataset tools that we write (for example, if we want to add functionality that randomly moves a camera in some range around a point, we'd want to ignore locations that are below the ground plane since collecting data through a surface is unrealistic). Another thing we can do to minimize useless data generation is provide users with parameters they can set to control how much variety/randomness they want in the data that's generated (for example, maybe users want to specify the range of angles/distances the camera should cover, or maybe they want to set a flag that skips scenes that have no labelled objects in them).

One other thing to keep in mind is that feature freeze for the Fortress release is about 1 month away (2021/09/07). So, if any of the dataset generation tools break API/ABI, we should probably work on those first so that the tools can be released with the accompanying sensors in Fortress.

I haven't followed the entire conversation, but I'll leave some pointers here that may hopefully help:

> GUI plugin

Before writing any code for the GUI plugin, I'd recommend creating a few sketches showing how the user is expected to interact with it. What buttons does it have? What goes where? What sequence of clicks is necessary to create a dataset?

> generates samples data from the scene without the control of the user

Depending on the datasets being created, this can be more convenient to use than a GUI plugin. For example, a user can choose a set of 1000s of objects that they want to generate data for, run that headless on the cloud and upload the resulting data to some cloud storage. This would make use of a server-side scene, rather than the GUI scene. (The distinction between server-side and client-side rendering plugins is described in the [Rendering plugins](https://ignitionrobotics.org/api/gazebo/5.1/rendering_plugins.html) tutorial.

That's why I think it's important to come up with a user story before deciding what approach to take. Is it better for the user to manually click through a GUI plugin to setup a scene, or is it better to run a script that runs everything automated with just some simple inputs, like the model URLs?

> ign-rendering vs ign-gazebo APIs

I'm assuming that for dataset generation, physics doesn't need to be running, right? If it needs to be running, I think using `ign-gazebo` APIs may make more sense. Otherwise, I don't think it matters. The difference would be whether we're creating entities that are part of the ECM and can be seen by other systems, or if we're creating rendering nodes that exist only in the 3D scene and are used only for the purposes of data generation. I can see both working, it just depends on the requirements for the tool.

for (1 to 1000)

We can start by porting Gazebo classic's [Distortion](https://github.com/osrf/gazebo/blob/gazebo11/gazebo/rendering/Distortion.cc) class over to the ogre 1.x implementation in ign-rendering. 

In ign-rendering, we can apply distortion to cameras using a similar approach as applying noise. The idea is to apply distortion as a render pass, see [example](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/examples/render_pass/Main.cc#L156-L166) for applying noise.

We'll need the add the abstract / base Distortion classes, see [GaussianNoisePass.hh](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/include/ignition/rendering/GaussianNoisePass.hh) and [BaseGaussianNoisePass.hh](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/include/ignition/rendering/base/BaseGaussianNoisePass.hh). 

Then put the actual ogre 1.x implementation in `ogre` directory, see [OgreGaussianNoise.cc](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/ogre/src/OgreGaussianNoisePass.cc) and [OgreGaussianNoise.hh](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/ogre/include/ignition/rendering/ogre/OgreGaussianNoisePass.hh)

There is a [macro](https://github.com/ignitionrobotics/ign-rendering/blob/ign-rendering6/ogre/src/OgreGaussianNoisePass.cc#L161) to register the render pass so that it can be created by the RenderPassSystem

Some quick answers. Ignition sensors produce data in the robot body frame: x forward, y left, z up. RViz expects camera image data to be in the optical frame: z forward, x right, y down.. We don't have an option to publish sensor data in optical frame right now in ign-sensors. That'll be nice to have. actually, they may all be from ign-transport: https://build.osrfoundation.org/view/ign-fortress/job/ign_transport-ign-11-win/25/

Yeah, there are a whole bunch that bleed in from transport and messages.  They go away with a newer version of protobuf, so I haven't invested a ton of time in squashing all of them (I can't even reproduce on my Windows machine).

In the meantime, a workaround for those who need to simulate lidars in an environment where a GPU is not available is to use `gpu_lidar` but with software rendering. Running `gz-sim` as is with a `gpu_lidar` in such an environment would currently cause a crash with an error: `[GUI] [Err] [Ogre2RenderEngine.cc:1098]  Unable to create the rendering window: ...`. The workaround is to set the environment variable `MESA_GL_VERSION_OVERRIDE=3.3` and `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=true` (this may not be necessary).

This is also how we have setup some of our CI machines (eg. Github Actions). There, since there is also no X server, we start one using `Xvfb`:

```
Xvfb :1 -noreset  -screen 0 1280x1024x24 &
export DISPLAY=:1.0
export MESA_GL_VERSION_OVERRIDE=3.3
```

The caveat with this workaround is that, unlike the `cpu_lidar`, it would still use visuals instead of collisions. The performance will also be poorer than `gpu_lidar`.

Found that the memory leak is caused in gz-rendering. 

@darksylinc if you could provide some quick comment and shed some light on the following piece of code, I'll then see if I can create a fix. I found that the vao manager continues to [create const buffers](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre2/src/Ogre2GzHlmsSharedPrivate.cc#L75) because [this condition](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre2/src/Ogre2GzHlmsSharedPrivate.cc#L64-L65) is always true. The pointers (`currPerObjectDataBuffer` and `lastMainConstBuffer`) are always being reset in [UnmapObjectDataBuffer](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre2/src/Ogre2GzHlmsSharedPrivate.cc#L108). Perhaps that if  condition for determining when const buffers need to be created has to be changed?

**Clarification:** `this->perObjectDataBuffers` is supposed to grow up to a certain point (how much depends on how many state swaps happen during render each frame) but at some point it should stabilize and afterwards more entries to `this->perObjectDataBuffers` are only rare or never happen again.

But with the current logic, it's growing indefinitely and without reuse after the frame is done, which is wrong.

Btw I think I'm seeing that we are never destroying those buffers on shutdown. It's not a big deal because OgreNext should deinitialize them for you; but it's for correctness' sake.

Hey,  I would like to work on this issue and have been working on implementing an example for a custom rendering sensor. 
I had quite a few clarifications to make about what I understood till now about the way rendering sensors present in `gz-sensors` use the `gz-rendering` library with `ogre`.

I apologize for asking such a silly question, but I am just getting started with understanding the implementation of rendering sensors and would like to confirm it so I do not make a mistake.
To find where exactly in `gz-rendering` I need to make changes to add bayer conversion function, I explored the codebase. 
I started with the normal camera sensor to get an initial understanding of the implementation of rendering sensors. Here's what I understood from the exploration:

* [Camera sensor](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/gz-sensors7/src/CameraSensor.cc) (`"gz/sensors/CameraSensor.hh"`): This is used to load the specific inputs given by the user from SDF elements into an instance of [camera rendering sensor](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/include/gz/rendering/Camera.hh)(present in `gz-rendering`), create an instance for a scene which updates the scene graph, calls appropriate methods for camera rendering sesnor to generate data and publishes image data on the protobuf image msg-type

* [Camera rendering sensor](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/include/gz/rendering/Camera.hh) (`"gz/rendering/Camera.hh"` and `gz/rendering/base/BaseCamera.hh`): This acts as connecting link between rendering engine generated scene graph and `gz-sensors camera`. This uses a pointer instance of the `RenderTarget` class to write the generated rendered image into a given image buffer and to define methods such as `PostRender` and `Update`.

* [BaseRenderTarget](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/include/gz/rendering/base/BaseRenderTarget.hh)(`"gz/rendering/RenderTarget.hh"` and `"gz/rendering/base/BaseRenderTarget.hh"`): This declares a class to represent `RenderTarget`, `RenderTexture`, and `RenderWindow`.
This class has definitions for pre-rendering and post-rendering procedures. 
* [ogreRenderTarget](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreRenderTarget.cc): This defines inherited classes of the above `BaseRenderTarget` class, `BaseRenderTexture` class and `BaseRenderWindow` class. This is where `Ogre::RenderTarget` is actually called to render the scene. It overrides the `Copy` method([`OgreRenderTarget::Copy`](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreRenderTarget.cc#L69)) that actually converts the underlying image to the specified format listed in the given Image using the `ogrePixelBox` function. I also found a comment stated under `OgreRenderTarget::Copy` for Bayer conversions to be implemented.

Here’s what I wanted to ask:
1. Am I headed in the right direction to infer the above ideas behind the implementation? 
2. Further, I couldn't find where the `OgreRenderTarget::Copy` or `OgreRenderTexture::Buffer` methods are called and where it actually converts the image format to, say, RGB to grayscale when simulation starts in gazebo. Could you please help me with that?
3. I also found some OgreSensors like [OgreCamera](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreCamera.cc) and [OgreDepthCamera](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreDepthCamera.cc). What are they used for?

thanks for working on this! Let me answer your questions below:

1. yes your understanding is correct. One thing to note is that by default gazebo launches with the `ogre2` render engine. Nonetheless, we can come up with a generic solution that can be re-used by different render engines.
2.  `OgreRenderTarget::Copy` is called by [`BaseCamera::Copy`](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/include/gz/rendering/base/BaseCamera.hh#L439) which is in turn called by CameraSensor [here]( https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/gz-sensors7/src/CameraSensor.cc#L577). As for converting from RGB to grayscale, the underlying render engine does that for us. As an example, in `ogre` render engine when we create a render texture, we give it an image format [here](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreRenderTarget.cc#L388-L390) (`ogreFormat`).  
3. `BaseCamera` as its name suggests is the base class for camera. You will find that its functions are virtual and overriden by derived classes such as `OgreCamera` and `Ogre2Camera` which is doing most of the work. `OgreDepthCamera` renders depth data stored in floating point image data. 

So going back to Bayer conversion. I think one implementation option would be to create a generic function `convertRGBToBayer`, e.g. in [Utils.cc](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/src/Utils.cc) and call that in `OgreRenderTarget::Copy` / `Ogre2RenderTarget::Copy`.

One thing to watch out for is that if user specifies a format like `BAYER_RGGB8`, currently gz-rendering does not know about this format, so the image format conversion functions like [here](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/ogre/src/OgreRenderTarget.cc#L364) will not work and we will need to catch that. We can just create RGB render texture in the underlying render engine and do Bayer conversions when we read back the values in `Copy`.

I think `ros2 topic hz` reports the rate in wall clock time and not sim time. So when the simulation is running slower than real time (with low RTF), you'll notice that the rate reported by `ros2` is lower than the target update rate. Sometime ago I wrote a script that checks the timestamps of the ros2 camera msgs and verified that they are correct. So I think the cameras should be hitting the target rate but in "sim time". There are things put in place in gz to make sure simulation is slowed down if the cameras are not able to hit their target update rate.

> What is causing the discrepancy between the gui rendering and server rendering?

gui rendering runs in a separate process from server and has its own thread for rendering. On the server side, all the rendering sensors perform updates in the same rendering thread. While some parallelizations are done on the GPU for the camera updates, there could still be other places where there is contention for resources, e.g. when reading data back from GPU to CPU, serializing and publishing the msgs.

> Is there a way to potentially bring up the server side sensor's update rate to match what is seen in the gui scene?

I think we would need to profile where the performance bottleneck is first. In the past, getting data from GPU to CPU had been slow for us. That could be something to look into. But I'm not sure if there's a workaround that can be done on the user side unfortunately (apart from running without a gui which didn't seem to help in your case).

> How to inspect topic publish rate in gz-garden with gz topic

I don't think that functionality is supported yet.

So in gazebo cameras do not actually update if there are no subscribers, hence the high RTF, i.e. no work is done because there are no consumers. It's only when you subscribe to the image topic e.g. through `gz topic -e` or `ros_gz` bridge, cameras start rendering and you get the fluctuations in RTF

As for the `--record` and `--playback` args, by default it works slightly different from rosbag. When you enable`-record`, it logs the clock topic, sdf data, and state (pose) of all objects to a database located in the path given by `--record-path`. You can then launch the sim in playback mode through `--playback` to replay the whole simulation. If you want more topics to be recorded, you'll need to specify them through the `record-topic` arg. I haven't tried running playback mode with the ros-gz-bridge before so not sure how well that works though.

Hey @iche033, I have opened PRs in four repositories. Here's a summary of the same.
The functionality reads the user input and renders an RGB image, which is later converted into a single channel 8bit Bayer image using `ConvertRGBToBayer()` added to [`Utils.cc`](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/blob/gz-rendering7/src/Utils.cc) inside `gz-rendering`.

* `gz-sensors` : Adds a switch case for `RGGB bayer format` inside `CameraSensor.cc` and passes the `R8G8B8` format to render the image.

> Is there a particular reason behind this change? I'd be interested to know.

For this change, we make use of [`std::expm1`](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/expm1)

Computes the e ([Euler's number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_(mathematical_constant)), 2.7182818...) raised to the given power num, minus 1.0. This function is more accurate than the expression [std::exp](http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/exp)(num) - 1.0 if num is close to zero.

> Additionally, the gazebo noise model adds an extra sign randomization step to the bias in :

This predates the inclusion of the rotors noise model, but my assumptions is that because the bias is drawn from a gaussian distribution specified by mean/stddev, we want to make sure that it can additionally be drawn as a positive or negative bias.

In the case that bias mean was 1, bias stddev is 0.1, there is also the chance that the bias may be centered around -1, which is handled by the sign flip.

> > Is there a particular reason behind this change? I'd be interested to know.
> 
> For this change, we make use of [`std::expm1`](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/expm1)
> 
> Computes the e ([Euler's number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_(mathematical_constant)), 2.7182818...) raised to the given power num, minus 1.0. This function is more accurate than the expression [std::exp](http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/exp)(num) - 1.0 if num is close to zero.
> 
> > Additionally, the gazebo noise model adds an extra sign randomization step to the bias in :
> 
> This predates the inclusion of the rotors noise model, but my assumptions is that because the bias is drawn from a gaussian distribution specified by mean/stddev, we want to make sure that it can additionally be drawn as a positive or negative bias.
> 
> In the case that bias mean was 1, bias stddev is 0.1, there is also the chance that the bias may be centered around -1, which is handled by the sign flip.

I think that would work. There's also a few more things that'll need to be done in order users to specify / change the type of distortion model to use in gazebo. That will likely have to happen through sdf, e.g.

```xml
<distortion type="brown">
   ...
</distortion>
```

In sdformat, we'll need to add a type attribute to distortion element:
https://github.com/gazebosim/sdformat/blob/7f63d022a48d3a224a3b7a777316c3822525c7b2/sdf/1.10/camera.sdf#L120

gz-sensors will need to parse this new `type` attribute, possibly when [creating a new image distortion model](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/7b4387fc64b12f72a39e7c7efafcbc8cc4230766/src/ImageDistortion.cc#L33). Currently there is the [ImageBrowDistortionModel](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/gz-sensors7/src/ImageBrownDistortionModel.cc) that uses rendering api to create the distortion effect and set it to the camera. I think we would need to add a new API to set the distortion type.

I recently hit this issue I'm wondering if there has been any improvements? The performance degradation on our sim after upgrading to ignition has been pretty profound. Before I'd head down a multi-threaded or multi gpu path it seems like the way ogre is being used is pretty simple, but that's probably not helping here.
 With the perf I was seeing I imagine that the code was doing a GPU readback right after each camera render, if that was the case there would be pretty significant penalties for multi-camera systems. GPU rendering always delayed from call submission, I've been experimenting with another rendering engine, and I've set it up for each camera to have their own independent frame buffer target, I am also doing readbacks with pixel buffer objects, by running all the camera rendering requests in serial and then using PBOs to read back the results the gpu has time to work while the CPU submits draw calls. 
 Replacing remotery with Tracy, which includes visualization of gpu draw call timing might help with future optimization of this system.

    - Create `UpdateRaycastCollisions()` into [`Physics.cc`](https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sim/blob/gz-sim8/src/systems/physics/Physics.cc)
        - Call `GetRaycastsFromLastStep()` feature to get the raycast results
        - Populate `RaycastResult` component data with output of this feature
        - Write component to ECM
    - Create system plugin `Raycast` that instanciates `RaySensor` and updates it with component data from ECM.

```python
import rclpy
import numpy as np
from rclpy.node import Node
from ros_gz_interfaces.msg import MaterialColor, Light
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
# ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge /world/default/light_config@ros_gz_interfaces/msg/Light@gz.msgs.Light
# ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge /world/default/material_color@ros_gz_interfaces/msg/MaterialColor@gz.msgs.MaterialColor
class lmTester(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('lm_tester_node')
        
        self.MaterialColorTopic = '/world/default/material_color'
        self.lightTopic = '/world/default/light_config'
        timer_period = 0.05
        self.timer = self.create_timer(timer_period, self.timerCallback)
        self.i=0
        self.delta=0.75
        self.ranges2=np.hstack((np.linspace(1-self.delta,1+self.delta,25),np.flip(np.linspace(1-self.delta,1+self.delta,25))))
        self.MaterialColorPub = self.create_publisher(MaterialColor,'{:s}'.format(self.MaterialColorTopic), 1)
        self.lightPub = self.create_publisher(Light,'{:s}'.format(self.lightTopic), 1)
        self.last_button = 0
    
    def timerCallback(self):

        if self.i < 49:
            self.i+=1
        elif self.i >= 49:
            self.i=0
        val2=self.ranges2[self.i]

        msgM=MaterialColor()
        msgM.entity_match=1
        msgM.entity.name="led_0"
        msgM.diffuse.r = 1.0
        msgM.diffuse.g = .1-.1*np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49+np.pi/2)
        msgM.diffuse.b = .1-.1*np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49+np.pi/2)
        msgM.diffuse.a = 1.0
        msgM.emissive=msgM.specular=msgM.ambient=msgM.diffuse
        self.MaterialColorPub.publish(msgM)
        msgM.entity.name="led_1"
        self.MaterialColorPub.publish(msgM)
        msgM.entity.name="led_2"
        self.MaterialColorPub.publish(msgM)
        
        msgL=Light()
        msgL.name="led_0"
        msgL.type=1
        msgL.diffuse.r = 1.0
        msgL.diffuse.g = .1-.1*np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49+np.pi/2)
        msgL.diffuse.b = .1-.1*np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49+np.pi/2)
        msgL.diffuse.a = 1.0
        msgL.specular=msgL.diffuse
        msgL.spot_inner_angle = 1.25+np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49)
        msgL.spot_outer_angle = 1.5+np.sin(2*np.pi*self.i/49)
        msgL.spot_falloff = 0.0
        msgL.attenuation_constant = 1.0
        msgL.attenuation_linear = 1.0
        msgL.attenuation_quadratic = 0.0
        msgL.intensity=5.0
        msgL.range=100.0
        self.lightPub.publish(msgL)
        msgL.name="led_1"
        self.lightPub.publish(msgL)
        msgL.name="led_2"
        self.lightPub.publish(msgL)

        return 
            
if __name__ == '__main__':
    rclpy.init()
    lmMT = lmTester()
    rclpy.spin(lmMT)
    lmMT.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()
```

I think it's just that the "visualization" is different but the depth image data encoding and depth values should be the same.  The image consists of float32 depth values. There doesn't seem to be a standard on how to display depth images. A quick look on the web shows both approaches being used in different places. Since the behavior in Gazebo has been around for a long time, I don't think we should change it. Perhaps a flag in the "Image Display" plugin to revert the colors could be an option.

I wrote some notes down not long ago on what sensors need optical frames:

>  Regarding optical frames, I looked back at what we did in subt and mbzirc and this is what I think:
> * we only need to use optical frame for regular RGB camera and depth camera images, e.g. /camera/image_raw and /camera/depth  topics. As an example, this was done in mbzirc: https://github.com/osrf/mbzirc/blob/main/mbzirc_ign/src/mbzirc_ign/model.py#L235-L260. We only created optical frames for image_raw and depth topics.
> * we don't need optical frames for point cloud topics, i.e. lidar point clouds and RGBD camera's point clouds, e.g. /lidar/points  or /rgbd_camera/points topics

The `optical_frame_publisher` sets this [transformation pose](https://github.com/gazebosim/ros_gz/pull/257/files#diff-f8a9d04c891ede310d8b02453045ded0a0bcb3b9f8d404c7799dd6555e987f86R163-R176) to create a z forward optical frame.

So if the above is true, instead of updating the generated sensor data itself, I think we just need a way to add an optical link with the above transformation inside gz-sim and set the msg frame id to that optical link name. 

Here's a proposal that's similar to option 2.

```xml
<sensor>
  <!-- Use the existing <frame_id> element (sdf 1.12+) to specify frame as usual -->
  <frame_id>my_z_optical_frame</frame_id>
  <!-- Support a new //sensor/frame element.
       Gazebo sees this and creates a new frame (link?) with the specified pose -->
  <frame name="my_z_optical_frame">
    <pose>0 0 0 -1.5708 0 -1.5708</pose>
  </frame>
</sensor>
```

Open to other ideas.

I think the issue in #29 was that the _frame_id_ in the RGBD pointcloud was populating with the _optical_frame_id_ too (there is only one field to define the frame in RGBD sensor). As long as the pcd (following ROS convention) and cameras (following cameras convention) don't get published on different frames, their information is going to be conflicting. Thanks to ROS tf tools, as long as you have the tf tree well defined, it does not matter too much the frame where the data is published as long as it is consistent.

IMO at least another frame tag should be added for RGBD.

Based on the comments above and in #29, the issue came from https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/pull/458 (and https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/pull/362 for DepthCameraSensor) since they incorrectly set the point cloud msg to optical frame. These PRs were supposedly submitted to fix "optical frame issues" for their use case. However, after gathering these recent comments I agree we should provide the ability to use a separate frame for the point cloud msg. 


One example would be to use `<frame_id>` and `<optical_frame_id>` for the separate frames:

```xml
<!-- sdf 1.12 -->
<sensor name="my_sensor" type="rgbd">
  <!-- point clouds will use this frame -->
  <frame_id>sensor_frame</frame_id>
  <camera>
    <!-- images will use this frame -->
    <optical_frame_id>optical_frame<opical_frame_id>
    ...
  </camera>
...
</sensor>
```

To achieve the above, we'll unfortunately need to revert #458 and #362, and un-deprecate the `<optical_frame_id>` tag in sdf 1.12. Not ideal since we're changing behavior yet again so I want to be very sure this is the right fix. Open to suggestions.

My main issue with using `<optical_frame_id>` is that it makes `frame_id` almost unnecessary. By that I mean, every `Image` and `CameraInfo` message would use the `optical_frame_id` instead of `frame_id` since that's what would be required in ROS. The only message that would use `frame_id` would be `PointCloud`. As we've seen in the past, this causes confusion because the most logical tag to specify the frame (`frame_id`) is almost always ignored. Also, since the frame specified in `optical_frame_id` would not actually exist in Gazebo as a frame (usually this would only exist in ROS via a static transform), consuming the `Image` message from other Gazebo systems/plugins would be problematic.

Generally, I think we should keep using the `frame_id` tag and the convention that we've used in Gazebo for frames. When bridging to ROS, that's when we should create the optical frame and convert to the ROS frame conventions. Ideally, the creation of an optical frame would be handled on the `ros_gz` bridge since it's only needed when using Gazebo with ROS. From the Gazebo side, we'd only have the `frame_id` tag and `ros_gz` would attach a `_optical` to the string used in `frame_id` and publish the `Image` and `CameraInfo` topics. It would also publish the necessary static transform to `/tf`.

I think the proposal to solve it in ros_gz is going in a good direction. However, I'm not sure if at the ros_gz level, there is enough information to correctly process it.

I'll try to explain.

Each (physical) camera has (in my view) 4 frames (the terminology is mine, do not try to google it):

1. The *mechanical* frame. This is a XYZ frame defining how the camera is mounted to the robot. Usually, this frame is in the middle of some mounting surface, in a tripod screw or somewhere similar. In Gazebo, it is usually a `<link>` with geometry and collisions.
2. The *geometrical* frame. This is a XYZ frame that denotes the optical center of the pinhole lens. I've seen implementations where this is an empty `<link>` in Gazebo and other implementations where this is `<sensor><pose>`.
3. The *optical* frame. This is a ZYX frame where the image lies in plane Z=0 and has the standard image coordinates Y down X right. This is what is proposed to be set by the `<optical_frame_id>` or its successor.
4. The *optical XYZ* frame. This is a XYZ frame that has the 90-0-90 rotation from optical frame.

You might be confused by the 4 frames and not 3. The reason why there are 4 frames is that e.g. in case the camera is mounted upside-down, the camera driver can be set to rotate the image by 180 degrees. Many cameras support this and many real use-cases do it so that image processing algorithms do not need to rotate the image. This rotation goes exactly between *geometrical* and *optical XYZ* frames. In the simple case with no rotation, both *geometrical* and *optical XYZ* frames are identical and that's why most people only think about 3 frames.

RGBD or multi-lens sensors would have a single *mechanical frame* and the other frames would be one for each lens.

In my ideal world, the assignment of the transforms in Gazebo would be:

1. *mechanical* = TF from `link/pose`, name from `link/name`
2. *geometrical* = TF from `sensor/pose`, name from `sensor/frame_id`
3. *optical XYZ* = TF from `camera/pose`, no name
4. *optical* = TF from `camera/pose` * 90-0-90, name from `camera/optical_frame_id` (could default to `sensor/frame_id + _optical_frame`)

This would be used for all pinhole sensors like RGB camera, Thermal camera and depth camera images (). Sensors like lidar and depth camera pointcloud would be happy with just *mechanical* and *geometrical* frames (thus utilizing `sensor/frame_id`). RGBD sensors could use the *optical* frame for images and *geometrical* frame for pointclouds.

Now, the problem is Gazebo would need the images published with *optical XYZ* frame (for which I don't have a name), while ROS would need them with *optical* frame. However, as the header in Gazebo messages is a KV store, we could easily store both (or all three) frames there.

(Un)fortunately, this touches a little bigger problem. That is transferring named frames from Gazebo to ROS. If something hasn't changed, only joints and model poses are transferred to ROS TFs (and only if you set up a TF bridge which is unfortunately undocumented anywhere (after my quick search for "ros_gz tf bridge")). However, as Gazebo also got the option of defining named frames, it would be useful to get these transferred to ROS, too.

If such mechanism were available, it seems to me a solution to this problem would be almost easy. `sensor/frame_id` would generate a named frame, `camera/optical_frame_id` would also generate a named frame and these frames would be published to ROS. This would alleviate users from having to either set up static TF publishers in ROS or code some C++ plugins for optical frame publishers. Of course it has problems with things like frame namespacing etc., but I guess the general idea should be clear, is it?

As a bonus, this would render unnecessary the current approaches I've seen where the optical center of the camera is represented by an empty link, just to get this frame to ROS. However, empty links connected via fixed joints make the whole simulation unstable. I've seen for example a camera sensor flying around a 2-ton robot I was designing. The only way to work it around was specifying the camera an unreasonable weight like 1 kg, where it has 40 g in reality. If we could transfer named frames to ROS, many of these empty links would just disappear.

> My main issue with using `<optical_frame_id>` is that it makes `frame_id` almost unnecessary. By that I mean, every `Image` and `CameraInfo` message would use the `optical_frame_id` instead of `frame_id` since that's what would be required in ROS. The only message that would use `frame_id` would be `PointCloud`. As we've seen in the past, this causes confusion because the most logical tag to specify the frame (`frame_id`) is almost always ignored. Also, since the frame specified in `optical_frame_id` would not actually exist in Gazebo as a frame (usually this would only exist in ROS via a static transform), consuming the `Image` message from other Gazebo systems/plugins would be problematic.

I can agree that this issue is due to the optical frame convention in ROS, which is not the whole scope of Gazebo.

> Generally, I think we should keep using the `frame_id` tag and the convention that we've used in Gazebo for frames. When bridging to ROS, that's when we should create the optical frame and convert to the ROS frame conventions. Ideally, the creation of an optical frame would be handled on the `ros_gz` bridge since it's only needed when using Gazebo with ROS. From the Gazebo side, we'd only have the `frame_id` tag and `ros_gz` would attach a `_optical` to the string used in `frame_id` and publish the `Image` and `CameraInfo` topics. It would also publish the necessary static transform to `/tf`.

This seems like a proper way to deal with it for ROS conventions, so it's an OK from me.

Adding more info:

Various places in the gz-sensors codebase calls [GetElement](https://github.com/gazebosim/sdformat/blob/1668f316e8e93c7f276d4bdbc46b75dd3ce066ac/include/sdf/Element.hh#L645) when parsing SDF parameters. This call creates a new element if one does not exist. Ideally, we should update the logic:
* If there is a check to see if an SDF element exists already (using `HasElement`), we can get element directly by calling  [FindElement](https://github.com/gazebosim/sdformat/blob/1668f316e8e93c7f276d4bdbc46b75dd3ce066ac/include/sdf/Element.hh#L670) 
* Alternatively, we can just call `FindElement` and check the returned `sdf::ElementPtr` if make sure it's not null.

There are many `GetElement` calls, it may be best to update them in separate PRs.
1.  examples, eg. `custom_sensor`: https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/8aff340be1c422e2898964c1ba62864c047fccb6/examples/custom_sensor/Odometer.cc#L56
2. Sensor classes, e.g. `LogicalCameraSensor.cc`: https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/8aff340be1c422e2898964c1ba62864c047fccb6/src/LogicalCameraSensor.cc#L101
3. Tests - quite a lot of them. The unit tests are in `src` dir, e.g. `ImuSensor_TEST.cc`: https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/8aff340be1c422e2898964c1ba62864c047fccb6/src/ImuSensor_TEST.cc#L172-L173
    while the integration tests are in `tests/integration`, e.g. `tests/integration/camera.cc`: https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/blob/8aff340be1c422e2898964c1ba62864c047fccb6/test/integration/camera.cc#L109

When processing both simultaneously, you would have to transform one into the frame of the other. In application code, you could not do the cheap approach of just flipping signs and order of axes as done here, because you would need to be able to handle any arbitrary transform between the frames or introduce unexpected limitations within your application.

Additionally, (as far as I understand) the user still has to manually create the static transformer. For my specific use case, I build multiple robots from the same URDF and just apply different configurations to achieve different robot and sensor setups. Perhaps this could better be fixed in `ros_gz` or specifically `ros_gz_bridge`, but I would strongly prefer if my simulation gave data comparable to my real-world sensors and would not require extra workarounds.

I traced this against current `gz-sensors` / `gz-sim` and would like to work on it, but there is one compatibility choice worth confirming before I change the frame semantics.

`MagnetometerSensor` already treats `SetWorldMagneticField(...)` as a vector in the Gazebo world frame and applies the sensor-pose inverse rotation. The missing conversion appears to be at the `gz-sim` call site: SDF defines `<magnetic_field>` in the frame established by `<spherical_coordinates>`, while the system passes that vector through unchanged. For ENU input, `SphericalCoordinates::LocalFromGlobalVelocity(...)` provides the heading-adjusted Gazebo-world vector directly, so the fix can remain in `gz-sim` without adding a second frame transform to `gz-sensors`.

The wrinkle is the later `use_earth_frame_ned` compatibility option from gazebosim/gz-sim#2460. Its current default deliberately preserves NED-valued output even though Gazebo's world frame is ENU. A full ENU-to-local transform would make the standards-correct `false` path straightforward, but applying it to the legacy `true` path would also change that flag's zero-heading axis convention.

My proposed regression matrix is:

- explicit world `<magnetic_field>`, heading 0° / 90°;
- generated field, `use_earth_frame_ned=false`, heading 0° / 90°;
- sensor yaw separated from world heading so the two rotations cannot cancel;
- comparison with the IMU named-frame heading behavior.

Would you prefer that the fix:

1. preserves the legacy NED axis convention and applies only the heading yaw to that path, while using the full ENU-to-local conversion for `use_earth_frame_ned=false`; or
2. introduces an opt-in compatibility parameter and makes all corrected paths represent a true Gazebo-world vector?

Once that compatibility boundary is confirmed, I can implement the bounded `gz-sim` change and tests.

> This is a known compatibility issue that occurs when using **Clang** with **libstdc++ 14** (GCC 14's standard library) in **C++17 mode**.
> 
> ### What exactly is the error?
> The error occurs when `zenoh-cpp` tries to use a `std::optional<zenoh::CancellationToken>`:
> ```
> error: the parameter for this explicitly-defaulted copy constructor is const, but a member or base requires it to be non-const
> ```
> Here's the technical breakdown:
> 1. Under the hood, `libstdc++-14` implements `std::optional` using a base class (`_Optional_payload_base`) that explicitly defaults its copy constructor with a `const` reference:
>    `_Optional_payload_base(const _Optional_payload_base&) = default;`
> 2. However, the type it's trying to wrap (`zenoh::CancellationToken`) does not have a standard `const` copy constructor (it's either move-only, or has a non-const copy constructor). 
> 3. **In C++17**, explicitly defaulting a special member function with a signature (`const&`) that doesn't match what the compiler would implicitly generate is **ill-formed**, resulting in a hard compile error in Clang. *(In C++20, this language rule was relaxed so it just silently marks the function as `deleted` instead of failing).*
> 
> ### Why is this happening now?
> Your `.github/workflows/bazel.yml` workflow is using a reusable workflow from `bazel-contrib` which by default runs on `ubuntu-latest` for Linux jobs. 
> GitHub recently updated `ubuntu-latest` from Ubuntu 22.04 to **Ubuntu 24.04**. 
> Ubuntu 24.04 ships with GCC 14. Even though your bazel test command overrides the compiler to Clang (`--repo_env=CC=clang --repo_env=CXX=clang++`), Clang still links against the system's default C++ standard library, which is now `libstdc++-14`. Combined with `--cxxopt=-std=c++17` in your `.bazelrc`, this creates the exact combination needed to trigger this compiler error.
> 
> ### How to fix it
> 
> There are a few ways to resolve this depending on what works best for your project:
> 
> **Option 1: Pin the CI runner to Ubuntu 22.04 (Recommended short-term fix)**
> You can bypass GCC 14 entirely by keeping the CI on Ubuntu 22.04. The `bazel-contrib` reusable workflow accepts an `os` matrix parameter. You can override it in your `bazel.yml`:
> 
> ```yaml
>   test:
>     uses: bazel-contrib/.github/.github/workflows/bazel.yaml@v7.7.0
>     with:
>       folders: |
>         [
>           "."
>         ]
>       # Tell the reusable workflow to use ubuntu-22.04 instead of ubuntu-latest
>       os: |
>         [
>           "ubuntu-22.04",
>           "macos-14"
>         ]
>       # ... your other settings ...
> ```
> 
> **Option 2: Use LLVM's `libc++` instead of GNU's `libstdc++`**
> Since you are explicitly using `clang` and `clang++` in the bazel command, you can instruct it to use LLVM's standard library which doesn't have this C++17 optional bug. Add this to your bazel test command:
> ```yaml
>       bazel_test_command: "bazel test --repo_env=CC=clang --repo_env=CXX=clang++ --cxxopt=-stdlib=libc++ --linkopt=-stdlib=libc++ --test_output=errors //..."
> ```
> 
> **Option 3: Compile with C++20**
> If the Gazebo ecosystem and its dependencies are ready to support C++20, you can change the standard in `.bazelrc`:
> ```diff
> - build --cxxopt=-std=c++17
> - build --host_cxxopt=-std=c++17
> + build --cxxopt=-std=c++20
> + build --host_cxxopt=-std=c++20
> ```
> This is the "most correct" long-term fix, but might not be feasible if other parts of Gazebo strictly require C++17 right now.

@facontidavide , thanks for the ideas and for joining the effort to improve performance 🏎️ . I'd like to suggest a different workflow:
 
 1. Use this issue as a meta issue. As you already noticed, the problem is complex and spans several repositories, and I'm happy to help: I've already merged changes that reduce copies with a clear performance gain. Since this is a serious effort, let's be ambitious and explore the idea of letting the GPU write sensor data straight into the transport's outgoing buffer, with the CPU writing only the small fields around it. I think that needs:
    * gz-transport: lend out the message buffer before publishing, ideally shared memory with a known, aligned layout, and tell the caller which mapping it lives in.
    * gz-rendering: per sensor compute passes that convert the render target to the message format (RGB, depth, point cloud, lidar ranges) and write it into the borrowed buffer. Maybe Vulkan is the target backend.
    * gz-sensors: write the small fields, then publish from a worker thread once the GPU is done, falling back to the CPU path when any piece is missing.
 
    In general we'd prefer to keep the discussion between humans, and use the agents for the implementation or to generate support materials (diagrams, benchmarks, etc.).

 2. Once we agree on the design and benchmarks, open PRs layer by layer, bottom up, to keep the load on reviewers and the buildfarm reasonable. Once the PRs are merged, we go ahead and open a new layer of PRs and so on.
 
 3. Celebrate!

Review follow-up (70b5f29): with horizontal resolution > 1, the message rows are the buffer rows, `RangeCount()` wide as its `count` says. The message holds the first RayCount×VerticalRayCount ranges, which is what main wrote before overrunning the message. This layout is now documented and pinned by `PublishMoreRangesThanRaysVertical`. Sizing the message for every range would change what is published, so I'm leaving that for a separate PR. The resolute CI failure is the CMake-warning quality gate (the same `gz-rendering-ogre` config warning on every recent gz-sensors PR); all tests pass there.

Review follow-up (f8b1e17):
- The byte-equality test now also covers an L8 frame (`PublishedBytesMatchCopyL8`), not just RGB.
- In-place publishing goes through a shared internal header `src/PublishInPlace.hh` (not installed). The same file is used by #693/#695/#696/#699. It builds the length-delimited head from a message instead of swapping fields out of the message and back.

Review follow-up (4a2b3c9): the local in-place helper is replaced by the shared internal header `src/PublishInPlace.hh`. It is byte-identical across the series (#693/#694/#696/#699), so the PRs merge in any order without conflicts in that file.

Review follow-up (f0e4fc7, 56fa435):
- New `RenderAheadMatchesSerial` tests: depth and GPU-lidar frames rendered ahead publish the same bytes and stamp as serial frames, and differ when the scene changes.
- The GPU lidar test also covers `SetScene` between `RenderAheadIfDue` and `Update`, and removing a pending sensor from a listener during `RunOnce` (it is skipped; the other lidar keeps publishing).
- The serial gates are tested too (image callback, lidar frame callback, noisy lidar).
- The per-sensor `renderedAhead` flags are replaced by a protected non-virtual `Sensor::DropRenderedAhead()`. This is ABI-safe because `Sensor` is pimpl'd and no data member was added.
- Depth/RGBD `SetScene` between the passes is not tested. Same-name depth cameras in two scenes share Ogre compositor definitions, and every teardown order hits either an `ItemIdentityException` or the HlmsDatablock assertion from #548.
